Installing artificial grass on a Gotha lot

In Gotha, installed synthetic grass runs $8–$18 a square foot, typically $10–$16, as of September 2026, the same published range as everywhere else. A half-acre or larger lot here is common enough that a residential quote often covers more square footage, more septic-tank planning and more open sun than a standard Orange County subdivision job does.

Reviewed by Luis Austin, owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026

Orange County's office, and what its code actually says

Gotha has no city government of its own, so a lawn conversion answers to Orange County's Division of Building Safety, reachable at 407-836-5550, with applications filed through the county's Fast Track Online Services. The county's Chapter 24 defines "turf" only as a list of living grass species, with no section written for a synthetic product, which leaves the county's ordinary landscape and drainage permitting, plus the state turf standard, as the written rules that actually apply.

A parcel search on the Orange County Property Appraiser -- parcel search confirms the taxing jurisdiction before a call goes out, since a Gotha-area mailing address can sit close enough to Ocoee or Windermere that the county line isn't always where a homeowner expects it.

Building above a sandy water table in Gotha

Gotha sits on native soil that's mostly fine sand, and after a heavy wet season that sand can stay saturated within a foot of grade far longer than most homeowners expect, sometimes well into the following month. A base built at the shallow end of the state's two-to-four-inch range barely lifts the turf above that saturation zone, so we lean toward the fuller depth on any lot where drainage already looks marginal before construction starts. The extra couple of inches doesn't change how the base is built, only how much separation exists between the turf and ground that's still holding last month's rain.

Sizing a lot that's closer to an acre than a quarter of one

Where a standard Winter Garden subdivision lot might run a fifth of an acre, plenty of Gotha addresses sit on a half-acre or more, a holdover from the community's citrus-grove past. A bigger lot changes the math on a full-yard conversion more than it changes the method: more square footage at the same $8–$18 range, more grading to plan across a larger fall, and often more existing shade from mature trees that were left standing when the grove around them was subdivided. The install method itself is no different from our standard residential process; Gotha just asks more of the grading step because of the acreage.

What the residential price range buys in Gotha

Installed synthetic lawn runs eight to eighteen dollars a square foot, with most yards landing between ten and sixteen. That range covers more than the turf roll itself: base material, compaction labor, seam tape and adhesive, and edge anchoring all sit inside the same number, and turf is typically under half of the total cost on a Gotha job. Paying toward the lower end of the range usually means a lighter product on a straightforward, flat, easy-access yard, while the upper end reflects a heavier face weight, tighter stitching, or a lot with tricky access that slows the crew down regardless of which product goes on top.

Say you have a half-acre former citrus lot

Say you have a 2,000 sq ft front and back yard on a half-acre Gotha lot where the grove that once stood there gave way to a house decades ago, and a septic tank sits near the side yard. At $8–$18 a square foot, a full conversion runs $16,000 to $36,000, and at the more typical $10–$16, most quotes land between $20,000 and $32,000. Locating the septic lid during the initial walk keeps the base plan from having to shift later, and the extra square footage compared with a standard subdivision lot is the main reason a Gotha quote often lands higher in total than a same-priced job on a smaller lot nearby.

Should a weed barrier go under a residential lawn?

A residential lawn in Gotha can go either way on a weed fabric layer between the compacted rock and the turf backing, and it's an optional add rather than something the build requires. Most owners choose to include it as a long-term guard against stray growth pushing up through a seam years down the road, and it makes no difference to how quickly the base itself drains. Dog runs are the one exception: fabric under a pet area traps liquid at the surface rather than letting it filter down into the rock, which is why that layer gets skipped entirely for pet turf even though it's standard on a plain family lawn.

Why a lawn can't cross a swale or hug a pond

Two setbacks apply to any Gotha lawn near water: turf has to stay at least ten feet from a natural or man-made waterbody unless a seawall or bulkhead already separates the two, and it can never go inside a drainage swale, ditch, or a stormwater pond's littoral zone, no matter how flat and convenient that strip of ground looks. Both rules exist because turf and the base under it change how water moves across a lot, and a swale or pond edge is specifically where the state doesn't want that changed. A yard backing onto a retention pond usually has more usable space than these setbacks first suggest, just not right up to the water's edge.

Septic-tank access on an older Gotha parcel

A number of Gotha's older, larger lots run on septic rather than a county sewer connection, which means the tank's pump-out lid has to stay reachable once turf and base material go down around it, a requirement that comes from the state turf rule itself rather than from any county add-on. Mapping that lid during layout, before the base gets built up around it, is a faster fix than relocating compacted rock later.

Topping off infill as a lawn ages

Infill goes in at roughly one to two pounds per square foot at installation, and that volume gradually drops over years of rinsing, rain, and UV exposure even on a lawn that's otherwise holding up well. A thin infill layer is one of the more common reasons an older Gotha lawn starts to look flatter or feel firmer underfoot than it did when new, since the backing loses some of the weight that kept blades standing upright. Topping it off periodically, rather than waiting until the lawn looks visibly bare in spots, keeps a ten- to twenty-year lifespan lawn performing closer to the higher end of that range.

Questions people ask

Does Gotha have its own building department, separate from Orange County?

No. Gotha has never incorporated, so Orange County's Division of Building Safety handles permitting for the entire community at 407-836-5550, the same office that covers the rest of unincorporated Orange County.

Do all Gotha homes have septic systems?

Not all, but enough of the older, larger lots do that it's worth checking before a quote assumes a county sewer connection. Newer estate infill closer to the Windermere line is more likely to run on county utilities.
